name: Atikamekw
confidence_why: Béland 1978, the only description of Atikamekw that mentions stress at all, presupposes a contrast between stressed and "weak (unstressed)" syllables and says retained final short vowels take a secondary stress, but never states where main stress falls, and Cooper 1945, Michelson 1939 and Sarazin 2020 are silent, so the placement of word stress is unknown.

catalog_quote: Short /i/, /a/ and /o/ are subject to a certain number of phonemic rules that sometimes neutralize completely their vowel quality. In weak (unstressed) syllables, short vowels are indiscriminantely centralized to -ʌ- or -ə-; e.g., the vowels /o/ in a:šokan 'bridge, pier, wharf' and /i/ in ašikan 'stockings' are phonetically identical. In the same syllable conditions, /a/ and /i/ are lowered to /o/ in the environment of -o-, -w- or -hw-; e.g. pa:štohwew 'he smashes him by tool'. Between the fricatives /š/ or after /n/ followed by a stop, /i/ is devoiced; e.g., o:šIššewa 'his father-in-law'; ṇta:niss 'my daughter'. In absolute final position, short vowels are usually deleted in polysyllabic words; e.g., /amiskwa/, amiskw 'beaver'. Exceptions are found, however, and not only in monosyllabic words; when occuring in this position, short vowels usually receive a secondary stress. E.g., niska 'goose'; maskwa 'bear'; mikko 'blood'; otehi 'heart'. The short final vowels /i/ and /a/ are kept in many particles; e.g., ekoši 'let's go'; ni:šitana 'twenty'. [Béland 1978: 302] ... In the final diphthongs, -aw, -ew, -iw, the second element is often syllabic, or else there is fairly balanced stress (cf. Bloomfield, 1930, 4,—in fact much more of what he records regarding Plains Cree, pp. 3-7, holds true for TB ...). [Cooper 1945: 40]

Exceptions are found, however, and not only in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Béland recognises stressed ('strong') versus weak/unstressed syllables (short vowels centralise to [ʌ]/[ə] in unstressed syllables) and says a short vowel that survives in absolute word-final position usually carries a secondary stress; he never states where primary word stress falls. The examples (niska, maskwa, mikko, otehi with final secondary stress) are consistent with non-final primary stress but the source does not say so. No placement rule can be read off this source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: retained word-final short vowels 'usually receive a secondary stress' (niska 'goose', maskwa 'bear', mikko 'blood', otehi 'heart').
new_statements.exceptions: None about primary stress (none stated). Final short vowels are usually deleted in polysyllables (amiskw 'beaver') but kept in many particles (ekoši 'let's go', ni:šitana 'twenty').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonemics of vowels in citation-form words); data from the three Atikamekw communities Manouane, Weymontachie, Obedjiwan, 1974-77. No mention of phrase-level accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Béland 1978 describes 'Atikamekw, a Cree dialect' of Manouane, Weymontachie and Obedjiwan (all three communities, 1974-77 fieldwork) = atik1240 as a whole; he notes Obedjiwan /r/~/l/ variation but treats one language. Cooper 1945 'Tête-de-Boule Cree' is the same language under its older exonym (Weymontachingue-area speakers).

(2) Sarazin 2020 Manuel d'initiation (54-page PDF, 3050-line txt covering the whole file): 'accent' occurs only at the text layerand 326 as 'accent circonflexe' marking long vowels (p. 12); no tonique/prosod/stress/intonation hit; the pronunciation section (pp. 10-13) treats consonant voicing, nasal-final -an/-in/-on/-en, final -w, silent letters and the deletion of unstressed /a/ in wapamew [wabmèo] but never states where stress falls — silent, agreed.
